assessment.text: On the full-year basis the premise holds, but only narrowly: membership fee revenue rose 11% against total revenue growth of 10.1%, a gap a modest slowdown could erase.

Part of that gap comes from a one-off: the September 2024 fee increase accounted for about 30% of membership income growth in 2026 and 40% in 2025, and because fees are recognized ratably that lift fades once the increase is fully in the base.

The record does not give fee revenue for the newest quarter, so the comparison mixes bases: Q4 revenue grew 11.1%, no slower than the fiscal-year fee figure of 11%, and the claim cannot be confirmed for the latest quarter.

Deferred revenue, where fees billed ahead would sit, grew 5.3% against revenue growth of 11.1%, so the corollary that it should outpace revenue fails; the record does not split deferred revenue into membership and other items, so this is a warning rather than a refutation.

For holding at the 2026-09-30 price, the step from this claim to the decision is unbacked: the price needs 17.3% revenue growth a year for 10 years at a 3.8% margin against 6.6% a year over the last three fiscal years, and fee revenue of $5,907 million inside $303.15B of revenue is too small to close that through growth alone.
Where the claim could matter is margin: at a 10.1% operating margin the same price needs only 2.9% a year, but nothing in the record shows fee income moving the margin toward that level.

case_for.text: Operating income outpaced revenue in Q4 and operating margin edged up by 0.1 points, which is consistent with a higher-margin fee stream growing faster, though the record does not attribute the gain to fees.
The filing names new sign-ups and Executive upgrades alongside the fee increase as drivers, so some of the fee growth does not depend on the price change.

case_against.text: With the fee increase supplying a declining but still large share of fee growth, fee growth stripped of it is likely at or below revenue growth, which turns the claim from a structural advantage into a timing effect.
Deferred revenue growing at less than half the pace of revenue is the opposite of what an accelerating fee base would leave on the balance sheet.

decides.text: Whether fee revenue keeps outgrowing total revenue once the 2024 fee increase has fully lapped, which only next year's fee disclosure can show.

assessment.text: The premise holds with real room: even the weakest of the four quarters, Q1 FY2026 at 3.7%, cleared the 3% bar by about five typical quarterly moves, and the test held in 19 of 20 readings over five years.

The margin's makeup is less sturdy than its level: gross margin subtracted 0.2 percentage points and the margin held only because operating expenses fell as a share of revenue.

An operating margin reaching the industry median of 5.0% would lower the growth the price needs to 13.0% a year, making relative growth less central to the decision.
Deferred revenue growing faster than revenue's 11.1% would suggest the growth lead is backed by advance billing rather than slowing.

analysis.corollary_rule: A corollary is an implication a model proposed and code computed. Each is read by the grammar and by the typed form the proposing model wrote: two readers, which is weaker than the two-of-three rule the thesis's own claims are read under. A corollary never moves a verdict; when most of a claim's computed corollaries come out against it, the claim is flagged.
analysis.audit_rule: A sentence is verified by code when every id it cites is in this run, at least one is evidence, and every number it writes is carried by that evidence: a verified finding's quotes and cited figures, an analytic's value, inputs and reading, a computed test's operands and result, a reported figure, an 8-K event's text. The claim's own words carry no number, and neither does the sentence a model wrote for a corollary: only what code computed for it does. A threshold is a third thing: when a number equals the threshold of a computed test or corollary the sentence cites, or a condition's own threshold, the sentence is not failed for it, and it is listed as a threshold restated, not checked as a fact. A bare year is carried by a cited item dated in that year. The audit does not decide whether a sentence follows from what it cites.
analysis.persistence_method: Resampling with replacement: 10,000 paths of 4 quarters, each step drawn from the measure's own last N quarterly changes (differences in points for a percent, growth rates for an amount), from the current value; the share of paths in which the test holds in every one of the 4 quarters. Seed 20261118. It assumes the past changes are exchangeable: it ignores trend, seasonality and anything not in the facts. It describes the history; it is not a forecast.

weakest_why.text: The company's own filing offers no peer growth or market-share data and concedes that some competitors have greater market penetration, so the claim cannot be confirmed from its disclosures.
The industry ranking gives only a modest edge: 8.2% against a class median of 7.2% in 2025, and a year earlier 5.0%, exactly at the median, so outgrowth is shown in one year only.
Even if Costco does outgrow its peers, that does not reach what the price needs. Of 44 ten-year spans of filers its size, 0 grew at 17.3% a year; the median was 1.3% and the 90th percentile 7.9%.

strongest_for.text: The margin floor is the sturdiest premise in the thesis. The test held in 19 of 20 past readings with room of 5.09x a typical quarterly move, and it held in 100% of resampled paths of its own past changes, which describes its stability, not a forecast.
Growth has picked up on the record: Q4 FY2026 revenue rose 11.1% against 8.1% four quarters earlier, and the newest quarter is the highest of the last eight.
Earnings are turning into cash, with 1.71x operating cash flow to net income, and free cash flow rose on the prior fiscal year. The business funds its own expansion.

strongest_against.text: The margin holds at its level but not through its makeup: gross margin subtracted 0.2 percentage points, and the margin held only because operating expenses fell as a share of revenue. That leaves the step from 3.8% toward the 5.0% median, which would lower the price's need, unbacked.

Part of the fee-growth lead is a one-off: the fee increase accounted for about 30% of membership income growth in 2026. Deferred revenue grew only 5.3% against revenue's 11.1%, a warning that prepaid billing is not keeping pace.

Free cash flow beating net income is a 0.10x-of-a-typical-move margin that held in 3 of 6 past readings. Management intends to raise capital spending to approximately $7,500 from $6,435, which presses on exactly that thin margin.

bottom_line.text: The thesis's three checked claims hold on this record, but none of them carries the decision. At the 2026-09-30 price the reverse DCF needs 17.3% revenue growth a year for 10 years, against the 6.6% a year the company grew over its last three fiscal years, and a margin floor, a narrow fee-growth lead and a thin cash cushion do not close that gap.
The claim closest to what the price needs, that Costco outgrows its peers, is unjudged. The only peer evidence puts it 4 of 9 on 2025 revenue growth, above the middle of its class but not leading it.

The implied growth leans most on the 3.8% margin assumption: at the industry median of 5.0% the need falls to 13.0%, and at the 90th percentile of 10.1% it falls to 2.9%. Yet Costco ranks 9 of 9 on operating margin in its class, so the lever that would justify the price is the one where it stands lowest.
At 45.7x earnings and a 2.2% free cash flow yield as of 2026-09-30, the holder is paying for growth or margin the filings have not yet shown, not for the cash the business returns today.
